title: The Butterfly That Knew the Way

pages.text: Every Tuesday morning at their school near the misty hills of Aburi, eight-year-old Nhyira and her friend Kojo met in the school pollination garden with Madam Serwaa. Bright red hibiscus, orange lantana and purple verbena flowers bloomed along the path. ‘Remember our first nature-club rule,’ Madam Serwaa smiled. ‘Scientists observe living creatures gently with their eyes and notebooks, we never chase, grab or touch a butterfly’s delicate wings.’

Bright red hibiscus, orange lantana and purple verbena flowers bloomed along the path.
‘Remember our first nature-club rule,’ Madam Serwaa smiled.
‘Scientists observe living creatures gently with their eyes and notebooks, we never chase, grab or touch a butterfly’s delicate wings.’
pages.alt: Eight-year-old Nhyira, Kojo and Madam Serwaa stand quietly beside blooming hibiscus and lantana flowers in a sunny Ghanaian school garden.

pages.text: As Nhyira watched a bright orange lantana cluster, a large black-and-yellow citrus swallowtail butterfly landed softly on a petal. Nhyira noticed a tiny triangle-shaped nick on the edge of its left back wing, probably from a bird’s beak. The butterfly uncoiled a long, curled tube under its head, its proboscis, and sipped sweet liquid nectar from the flower like a tiny drinking straw!

The butterfly uncoiled a long, curled tube under its head, its proboscis, and sipped sweet liquid nectar from the flower like a tiny drinking straw!
pages.alt: Close view of a black-and-yellow swallowtail butterfly with a tiny notch on its left wing sipping nectar through its uncoiled proboscis.

pages.text: When the school bell rang, the swallowtail fluttered high over the mango trees and disappeared. The next morning before assembly, Nhyira checked the exact same lantana bush, and gasped! Sitting on the same branch was the very same black-and-yellow butterfly with the tiny triangle notch on its left wing. ‘Madam Serwaa!’ Nhyira whispered. ‘How did a butterfly with a brain smaller than a grain of rice find its way back here?’

‘How did a butterfly with a brain smaller than a grain of rice find its way back here?’
pages.alt: The next morning, Nhyira points excitedly from a safe distance as the same notched-wing swallowtail lands on the lantana bush.

pages.text: Madam Serwaa opened a science picture card showing a butterfly’s head up close. ‘First, a butterfly senses the world very differently from us,’ she explained. ‘Its two rounded compound eyes are made of thousands of tiny lenses that can see wide around it, and can even see ultraviolet light patterns on flower petals that are completely invisible to human eyes! Those ultraviolet markings point straight to the nectar like airport runway lights.’

Those ultraviolet markings point straight to the nectar like airport runway lights.’
pages.alt: Madam Serwaa shows Nhyira and Kojo an illustration of a butterfly’s compound eyes and ultraviolet bullseye patterns on a flower.

pages.text: ‘What about its two feelers?’ asked Kojo. ‘Those are its antennae,’ said Madam Serwaa. ‘A butterfly smells with its antennae! Microscopic scent sensors on the antennae detect the sweet perfume of flowers and the exact leaf scent of the citrus or lime trees where a mother swallowtail lays her eggs. And when a butterfly lands on a leaf, taste sensors on its feet tell it immediately whether that plant is the right food for its caterpillars!’

pages.alt: The swallowtail butterfly touches a green lemon leaf with its feet and waves its club-tipped antennae.

pages.text: ‘As the butterfly sips nectar,’ Madam Serwaa continued, ‘yellow dust called pollen sticks to its body and gets carried to the next flower, helping plants make seeds and fruit!’ Then Kojo asked, ‘Do all butterflies in Ghana fly thousands of kilometres across the world like the famous monarch butterflies we saw in a library book?’ Madam Serwaa shook her head. ‘No, Kojo, that is a very important scientific distinction!’

‘No, Kojo, that is a very important scientific distinction!’
pages.alt: Yellow pollen grains cling to the butterfly as it flies between flowers while Madam Serwaa explains local vs migrating species.

pages.text: ‘Only a few butterfly species in the world make giant cross-continent migrations,’ Madam Serwaa explained. ‘Ghana is home to more than 900 butterfly species! Some move seasonally with the rains, while many garden and forest butterflies, like our citrus swallowtail, live right in a local habitat. To find their way around their neighbourhood, they use the position of the Sun in the sky, polarized light, scent trails and familiar shapes of trees and bushes.’

pages.alt: A wide view of the sunny school garden shows the swallowtail orienting by the morning sun, mango trees and flower beds.

pages.text: ‘Do scientists know everything about how tiny insect brains do that?’ Nhyira asked. ‘Not yet!’ smiled Madam Serwaa. ‘We know butterflies combine sun-compass cues, ultraviolet sight and antennae smell, but neurobiologists are still discovering how such a tiny brain weaves all those clues into a mental map!’ For fifteen minutes, Nhyira and Kojo stood still and tallied every butterfly visit: 6 yellow grass butterflies, 4 black-and-yellow swallowtails and 5 white butterflies, 6 plus 4 plus 5 equals 15 visits in all!

pages.alt: Nhyira and Kojo count tally marks on their clipboard as yellow, white and swallowtail butterflies visit the garden flowers.

pages.text: Before going inside, Nhyira watered a row of young lime and hibiscus seedlings and wrote in her nature book: What Would You Build, Discover or Change? ‘If we plant native nectar flowers and never spray harmful chemicals on our school garden,’ she said, ‘the butterflies will always have a safe home to return to.’ What living creature in your compound or schoolyard could you observe quietly and protect this week?

activities.question: Which body parts does a butterfly use to smell flower scents and taste whether a leaf is the right host plant?
options: It smells with its antennae and tastes with sensors on its feet
It smells with its wings and tastes with its ears
It uses a glass magnifying lens
activities.explanation: Butterflies detect scents with receptors on their antennae and taste plant chemicals with contact chemoreceptors on their feet (tarsi).

activities.definition: Fine yellow powder made by flowers that insects carry from blossom to blossom so plants can make seeds and fruit
distractors: Small pebbles at the bottom of a river
Drops of rain falling from a dark cloud

activities.question: Do all butterflies in Ghana migrate thousands of kilometres across continents like the North American monarch butterfly?
options: No; most Ghanaian butterflies live and navigate within local habitats
Yes, every single butterfly flies to the North Pole every night
No, because butterflies cannot fly at all
activities.explanation: Different butterfly species have different behaviours; most local garden and forest butterflies navigate within a local habitat rather than migrating across continents.

activities.question: Nhyira and Kojo counted 6 yellow grass butterflies, 4 swallowtails and 5 white butterflies. How many butterfly visits did they tally in total?

activities.prompt: Put Nhyira’s scientific investigation in order.
items: Nhyira notices a swallowtail with a tiny wing notch sipping nectar.
She sees the same butterfly return the next day and asks how it navigated.
She and Kojo tally 15 butterfly visits and plant more nectar flowers.

activities.prompt: How does watching animals quietly without hurting them help you learn more about nature?

glossary.definition: A butterfly’s long, coiled feeding tube that unrolls like a straw to sip liquid nectar from flowers
Made of many smaller parts; an insect’s compound eye has thousands of tiny lenses working together
The pair of sensitive feelers on an insect’s head used to detect smells, air movement and balance
Fine powder produced by flowers that is transferred by pollinators to fertilise other flowers
